article_title: How to Learn Python in 30 Days — Complete Beginner Roadmap
claim: Average Python developer salary in India: ₹5 – 18 LPA.
source: Indeed India — Python Developer Salaries
required_correction: Salary aggregators (Indeed, Glassdoor, WSCubeTech) place the national average around ₹5.8 LPA, with freshers closer to ₹3–5 LPA and only senior/specialized (AI/ML) roles reaching ₹15–18+ LPA. The article's ₹5–18 LPA framing reads as a single 'average' when it is really the low-to-high spread across experience levels; reframe accordingly and note there is no official government wage survey for this specific role, so all figures are industry estimates.

article_title: How to Learn Python in 30 Days — Complete Beginner Roadmap
claim: Python is the most beginner-friendly programming language in the world.
required_correction: Subjective ranking claim (some educators would point to Scratch or JavaScript for absolute beginners). Fine to keep as framing/opinion but should not be presented as a settled fact.

article_title: How to Learn Python in 30 Days — Complete Beginner Roadmap
claim: FreeCodeCamp Python course on YouTube — 4.5 hours, covers everything
source: freeCodeCamp — Ultimate Beginner's Python Course
required_correction: freeCodeCamp's 'Learn Python – Full Course for Beginners' YouTube video runs about 4 hours 26 minutes, consistent with the ~4.5-hour claim. Note freeCodeCamp also publishes longer Python courses (6–13+ hours) under similar branding on the same channel, so the article should name the exact video title to avoid readers landing on the wrong one.

article_title: How to Learn Python in 30 Days — Complete Beginner Roadmap
claim: Thirty minutes doesn't feel like much in the moment, but over 30 days it's 15 hours of focused practice.
source: Self-verified arithmetic (0.5 hr × 30 days = 15 hr)
required_correction: Arithmetic is correct, no factual error. Internal consistency note: the Week 1 section earlier tells readers to budget 1–2 hours/day, so this later '30 minutes a day' framing contradicts the roadmap's own stated daily commitment.

article_title: How to Learn Python in 30 Days — Complete Beginner Roadmap
claim: The most common drop-off point is around day 10 to 12, right as loops and functions start combining into slightly more complex logic.
required_correction: Stated as an established pattern but no learning-platform completion data, study, or citation supports the specific 'day 10–12' figure. Either cite real completion-rate data from a MOOC/course provider or reframe as the author's own observation/opinion rather than fact.

article_title: How to Learn Python in 30 Days — Complete Beginner Roadmap
claim: Learning alongside even one other person... measurably improves follow-through compared to studying entirely alone.
required_correction: The word 'measurably' implies a specific study or statistic, but none is cited. General accountability/peer-learning research exists in education literature, but this article references none. Soften to opinion/experience framing or add a real citation.

article_title: Credit Score in India: How It Works and How to Fix a Bad One
claim: Fifty to seventy points — that's roughly what a single credit card bill, paid just five days late, can cost you.
source: Bajaj Housing Finance — Impact of Late Payment on CIBIL Score; Tata Capital — Late Payments Impact Credit Score
required_correction: The 50–100 point drop figures repeated across lender resources are tied to a payment reported as delinquent to the bureau, which generally means the account is roughly 30+ days past due — most card issuers do not report a missed payment to CIBIL until around the 30-day mark. A bill paid 5 days late may incur a late fee/interest but typically is not even reported as a missed payment, so it would not plausibly cause a 50–70 point drop. Correct the article to tie the point-loss figure to a payment still unpaid at ~30 days past due, not 'five days late.'

article_title: Credit Score in India: How It Works and How to Fix a Bad One
claim: Your credit score (most commonly your CIBIL score) ranges 300-900.
source: TransUnion CIBIL — What is CIBIL Score?
required_correction: None needed — the 300–900 range for CIBIL TransUnion scores is accurate and matches CIBIL's own published documentation.

article_title: Credit Score in India: How It Works and How to Fix a Bad One
claim: Above 750 is generally considered good and unlocks better rates; below 650 makes approval harder and more expensive.
source: TransUnion CIBIL — Free CIBIL Score and Report
required_correction: Consistent with widely published lender score bands (750+ generally treated as good/prime, below 650 as higher-risk). No correction needed, though exact bank-by-bank cutoffs vary and aren't fixed by CIBIL itself.

article_title: Credit Score in India: How It Works and How to Fix a Bad One
claim: Factor weight table: Payment history ~35%, Credit utilization ~30%, Credit history length ~15%, Credit mix ~10%, New credit inquiries ~10%.
source: TransUnion CIBIL (official position: methodology is proprietary, exact weights not published) vs. myFICO — How FICO Scores Are Calculated
required_correction: This exact 35/30/15/10/10 breakdown is the U.S. FICO score model's published weighting, not CIBIL's. TransUnion CIBIL has publicly stated that its scoring algorithm and exact factor weightings are proprietary and not disclosed — it confirms payment history and utilization are the most influential factors but does not publish precise percentages (third-party finance blogs give varying, unofficial estimates such as 30/25/25/20, which also don't match this table). The article must stop presenting FICO's exact U.S. figures as CIBIL's documented India-specific methodology. Replace with: CIBIL considers payment history, utilization, credit age, credit mix, and inquiries as the main factors, but does not publish exact weights — and if illustrative percentages are used, they must be explicitly attributed to FICO's U.S. model, not CIBIL's.

article_title: Credit Score in India: How It Works and How to Fix a Bad One
claim: Keep the amount you owe below 30% of your total available credit limit; below 10% is even better if trying to raise your score before a big loan application.
source: Bajaj Finserv Markets — CIBIL Score Calculation
required_correction: The sub-30% utilization guideline is a widely repeated industry rule of thumb across Indian lender/fintech resources, but — like the weight table — it is not an official CIBIL-published threshold. Keep as practical guidance but frame it as a common recommendation, not a documented CIBIL rule. The under-10% 'ideal' figure is even less standardized and should be flagged as an aggressive personal target rather than an official benchmark.

article_title: Credit Score in India: How It Works and How to Fix a Bad One
claim: CIBIL, Experian, or Equifax all offer at least one free credit report check per year.
source: RBI-mandated Free Full Credit Report (FFCR) rule, effective January 1, 2017, reported by Business Standard
required_correction: Accurate — RBI mandated in 2016 (effective Jan 1, 2017) that every Credit Information Company provide one free full credit report per calendar year to individuals with a credit history on file. Minor gap: India has a fourth CIC, CRIF High Mark, also covered by this mandate, which the article omits alongside CIBIL, Experian, and Equifax.

article_title: Credit Score in India: How It Works and How to Fix a Bad One
claim: A single late payment typically recovers within 3-6 months of consistent on-time payments; a pattern of missed payments or a default takes 12-24 months to rebuild.
source: Freed — Late Payment Impact on Credit Score; CreditMantri — Does Making Late Payments Affect the CIBIL Score
required_correction: Fintech/lender resources generally cite 6-12 months for recovery from a single late payment (somewhat longer than the article's 3-6 month claim), and there is no consistent published figure for the 12-24 month default-recovery timeline — estimates vary widely across sources and none are officially published by CIBIL. Flag both ranges in the article as rough approximations rather than precise, sourced timelines.

article_title: Credit Score in India: How It Works and How to Fix a Bad One
claim: A serious default can remain visible on your credit report for years.
source: Tata Capital — Late Payments Impact Credit Score: Effect on CIBIL & Fixes
required_correction: Accurate but imprecise — CIBIL retains default/delinquency records for approximately 7 years from the date of first default. The article could be strengthened by stating the specific 7-year figure instead of the vaguer 'for years.'

article_title: Credit Score in India: How It Works and How to Fix a Bad One
claim: Checking your own score through a credit bureau's official free-check service or most banking apps is a 'soft inquiry' and has no effect on the score.
source: TransUnion CIBIL — Free CIBIL Score and Report
required_correction: Accurate and well-established: self-initiated checks are soft inquiries that do not affect the score; only lender-initiated hard inquiries (as part of a credit application) can. No correction needed.

article_title: Credit Score in India: How It Works and How to Fix a Bad One
claim: Your salary has nothing to do with your credit score directly — Indian credit scores are built entirely from borrowing and repayment behavior, not income.
source: TransUnion CIBIL — All You Need to Know About Your CIBIL Score
required_correction: Accurate — CIBIL scores are derived purely from credit bureau data (loan/card accounts and repayment history reported by lenders), not income. Income is assessed separately by lenders when deciding loan amount/eligibility, but it is not a bureau score input. No correction needed.

article_title: How to Set Up Parental Controls Without Making a Teenager Furious
claim: Google's Family Link on Android and Apple's Screen Time on iOS both let you set daily app time limits, downtime windows, app-specific blocks, and content filtering by age rating on app stores.
source: Google Families Help — Manage your child's Google Play apps; Apple Support — Use Screen Time to manage your child's iPhone or iPad
required_correction: Accurate description of both platforms' core feature sets (app time limits, downtime/schedules, content filtering by age rating). No correction needed.

article_title: How to Set Up Parental Controls Without Making a Teenager Furious
claim: Both Family Link and Screen Time also show a weekly activity report to the parent.
source: Google Guidebooks — Set App Limits with Family Link
required_correction: Accurate — both platforms generate a periodic (weekly) screen-time activity summary visible to the parent. No correction needed.

article_title: How to Set Up Parental Controls Without Making a Teenager Furious
claim: Both require setting the child's account up as supervised initially, a one-time setup, not an ongoing hassle.
source: Google Families Help — Add & manage supervision on a current Google Account
required_correction: Accurate for Family Link's supervised-account setup; Apple's equivalent runs through Family Sharing/Child Accounts. Minor overstatement: calling it strictly 'one-time' understates that supervision settings can and often need to be revisited as the child ages, which the article's own later sections (on scaling down controls) actually acknowledge — worth reconciling the two sections.

article_title: How to Set Up Parental Controls Without Making a Teenager Furious
claim: Family Link and Screen Time are built around a single primary user per device, so shared family tablets/computers need separate user profiles for controls to apply correctly.
required_correction: Plausible given both platforms' per-account design, but this specific claim about shared-device behavior could not be independently confirmed against current Google/Apple documentation within available research. Verify against current Family Link and Screen Time support docs before publishing, since device-sharing behavior is the kind of detail that changes across OS updates.

article_title: How to Set Up Parental Controls Without Making a Teenager Furious
claim: Escalating restrictions without a conversation tends to produce a more determined workaround next time instead of actual behavior change.
required_correction: Reasonable parenting/behavioral judgment but not an independently checkable claim — no child-development study is cited. Fine as opinion; should not be implied to be research-backed.

article_title: How to Set Up Parental Controls Without Making a Teenager Furious
claim: Most teenagers already know, and often admit privately, that late-night scrolling affects their own sleep and mood the next day.
required_correction: Presented as an established fact about teen self-awareness with no citation. Sleep-science literature does link screen use to sleep disruption generally, but the specific claim that teens 'often admit privately' this is anecdotal framing with no source — either cite an actual survey/study or reframe as the author's assumption.

article_title: How to Set Up Parental Controls Without Making a Teenager Furious
claim: Scripted dialogue sections (e.g., 'What to Say When They Ask Don't You Trust Me?', the group-chat/social-pressure response) presented as practical advice.
required_correction: Reads as generic, template-style advice with no first-hand attribution (no named parent, no specific situation) — likely fabricated/generic rather than genuine lived experience. Should be clearly framed as suggested scripts/general guidance, not implied as tested, real-world dialogue from an actual parent.

article_title: How to Verify a Company Is Real Before Accepting a Job Offer
claim: Go to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs website (mca.gov.in) and use the 'Check Company/LLP Master Data' search under the MCA Services section.
source: Vakilsearch — MCA Master Data: Check Company & LLP Details on V3 Portal
required_correction: mca.gov.in is the correct domain and the master-data lookup is a real, free government service, but the current official menu item on the MCA V3 portal is labeled 'View Company/LLP Master Data,' not 'Check Company/LLP Master Data.' Update the exact menu wording so readers can locate it.

article_title: How to Verify a Company Is Real Before Accepting a Job Offer
claim: The MCA search returns the company's CIN, date of incorporation, registered office address, and current status (active, dormant, or struck off).
source: ebizfiling — MCA Master Data: Company Search, ROC Records & Usage Guide
required_correction: Accurate — these are the standard fields returned by the MCA master data search. No correction needed.

article_title: How to Verify a Company Is Real Before Accepting a Job Offer
claim: If the company mentions a GSTIN, verify it on the GST portal (services.gst.in) under Search Taxpayer.
source: Goods & Services Tax (GST) official government portal — Search Taxpayer service
required_correction: CRITICAL ERROR at the center of a fraud-prevention article: 'services.gst.in' is not the real GST portal — the domain does not even resolve (DNS lookup returns ENOTFOUND; it is not a live, registered site at all). The actual official GST Search Taxpayer service is at https://services.gst.gov.in/services/searchtp, part of the government's gst.gov.in domain operated by GSTN. Directing readers who are trying to verify a potential scam employer to a dead/wrong domain is especially damaging given the article's entire premise is fraud prevention — this must be corrected to services.gst.gov.in before publishing, and the article should also warn readers to double-check they are on a *.gst.gov.in domain generally, since lookalike GST domains are a known phishing pattern.

article_title: How to Verify a Company Is Real Before Accepting a Job Offer
claim: Google the exact office address given — does it map to a real, occupied commercial space, or a residential flat, or nothing at all?
required_correction: Practical due-diligence advice/heuristic, not itself a checkable factual assertion. No source needed.

article_title: How to Verify a Company Is Real Before Accepting a Job Offer
claim: The EPFO member portal lets you check an establishment's registration status by name, and checking whether a company actively remits provident fund contributions is a strong, hard-to-fake signal.
source: EPFO — Establishment Search (Unified Portal, Employer)
required_correction: The establishment search tool does exist and is genuinely useful for this purpose, but the article's label 'EPFO member portal' is imprecise — this lookup lives on EPFO's employer/establishment search tool (unifiedportal-emp.epfindia.gov.in), distinct from the member/UAN portal (unifiedportal-mem.epfindia.gov.in) that employees use for their own PF passbook. Correct the terminology so readers land on the right tool.

article_title: How to Verify a Company Is Real Before Accepting a Job Offer
claim: Check how long the domain has existed using any public WHOIS lookup tool.
source: ICANN — WHOIS Lookup
required_correction: Accurate — public WHOIS/RDAP lookup tools do show domain registration/creation dates (subject to WHOIS privacy redaction in some cases). No correction needed.

article_title: How to Verify a Company Is Real Before Accepting a Job Offer
claim: A company that runs a formal background verification on you is usually a positive signal rather than a red flag.
required_correction: Reasonable heuristic but a subjective judgment call about what a given practice signals, not an independently checkable fact.

article_title: How to Verify a Company Is Real Before Accepting a Job Offer
claim: Fake job offers tend to spike whenever hiring activity in a sector is picking up, since scammers deliberately mimic real hiring surges.
required_correction: Presented as an established pattern with no data, study, or fraud-report citation. Plausible but unverified in available research — either cite a real fraud statistics source (e.g., India's Cyber Crime Coordination Centre/I4C reports) or reframe as the author's inference rather than established fact.

article_title: How to Verify a Company Is Real Before Accepting a Job Offer
claim: Verifying a company before you accept its offer takes about fifteen minutes and doesn't require any special access.
required_correction: Specific time estimate stated as fact with no basis given. The number of checks the article itself lists (MCA, GST, WHOIS, LinkedIn, Glassdoor/AmbitionBox, EPFO, calling HR) would plausibly take considerably longer than 15 minutes if done thoroughly. Remove the precise figure or soften to a rough range.

article_title: How to Turn Off Ads in Free Android Apps — What Is Legal and What Is Not
claim: Downloading a 'mod APK' that claims to have ads pre-removed is copyright infringement on the developer's side, and violates the terms of service you agreed to when you first installed the real app.
source: law.asia — Reverse Engineering and India's Copyright Act; SpicyIP — Is Decompilation of Software Legal Under the Indian Copyright Act
required_correction: Directionally correct — unauthorized reverse-engineering and redistribution of a copyrighted app likely infringes under India's Copyright Act, 1957 (as amended in 2012 to add anti-circumvention/technological-protection-measure provisions), and separately breaches the app's ToS as a contract matter. But the article asserts this as flat legal fact with zero citation to any actual statute or case. It should name the legal basis (Copyright Act 1957, the 2012 anti-circumvention amendment) and note that Indian law does recognize a fair-use/interoperability exception for reverse engineering — which does not cover redistributing a modified app to others, a distinction the article never draws.

article_title: How to Turn Off Ads in Free Android Apps — What Is Legal and What Is Not
claim: Using root access to patch out an app's ad SDK for personal use is a gray area, but distributing that patch or the patched app to others crosses clearly into copyright and platform policy violation.
source: law.asia — Reverse Engineering and India's Copyright Act
required_correction: Broadly consistent with how Indian copyright law treats unauthorized reproduction/distribution vs. narrower personal-use reverse engineering, but again stated with no citation to the actual statute. Reference the Copyright Act 1957 (as amended) directly instead of asserting the legal conclusion as if self-evident.

article_title: How to Turn Off Ads in Free Android Apps — What Is Legal and What Is Not
claim: Network-level ad blocking (apps/Private DNS blocking ad domains) doesn't alter the app's code or violate copyright, and is generally treated as acceptable personal use in India.
required_correction: No Indian statute, regulation, or case law specifically addressing the legality of DNS/network-level ad blocking could be located. The underlying logic (no code is modified, nothing copyrighted is redistributed) is reasonable, but 'generally treated as acceptable... legal' is stated as settled law with zero citation — the same unsupported-legal-claim pattern flagged for the whole article. Either find a real source discussing ad-blocker legality in India specifically, or reframe this section as informed inference rather than a legal conclusion.

article_title: How to Turn Off Ads in Free Android Apps — What Is Legal and What Is Not
claim: Google's Play Store developer policies cap how intrusive ads are allowed to be, restricting full-screen interstitials at certain moments and banning ads that mimic system notifications.
source: Google Play Console Help — Understanding Google Play's Better Ads Experiences policy
required_correction: Accurate — Google's Better Ads Experiences policy (effective September 30, 2022) restricts full-screen interstitial ads at app launch/level transitions (with a rewarded, opt-in ad exception) and prohibits ads disguised as system UI/notifications. No correction needed; citing the specific policy name would strengthen the article.

article_title: How to Turn Off Ads in Free Android Apps — What Is Legal and What Is Not
claim: Android lets you delete or reset your advertising ID under Settings > Privacy > Ads, and separately opt out of ads personalization.
source: Google Play Console Help — Advertising ID
required_correction: Accurate for Android 12+ devices. Minor note: the exact menu depth/label varies by Android version and OEM skin (e.g., newer stock Android nests it under Settings > Privacy & security > Ads, some OEM skins under Settings > Google > Ads), so this path may drift out of date and should be periodically re-verified against the current Android version.

article_title: How to Turn Off Ads in Free Android Apps — What Is Legal and What Is Not
claim: Modified/cracked APKs are a common vector for malware, since there's no verification process behind these files the way there is on the Play Store.
source: Google Play Protect / general Android security industry reporting on sideloaded APK risk
required_correction: Well-established in security research and Google's own Play Protect reporting that apps distributed outside official stores (including modified/cracked APKs) carry substantially higher malware rates, since they bypass Play Protect's automated scanning. No correction needed, though citing a specific Google Android security transparency report would strengthen the claim's sourcing.
